pages.name: The starting current
pages.task: A motor takes 100 A at full load. Started direct on line, roughly what current does it draw at first?
pages.why: 6 to 8 × 100 A gives 600 to 800 A, so about 700 A. The current stays high until the motor reaches about 75% of its speed.[^1]

pages.text: A big motor's start is a sudden, heavy load. Here it takes 600 kVA from a 630 kVA set. At first, only the small sub-transient reactance holds the current back, say 0.15 per unit. A load drawing the set's own 630 kVA at full voltage is 1 per unit. A bigger load is a smaller impedance. So the motor's starting impedance is 630 ÷ 600 = 1.05 per unit. The two share the voltage like a divider. The motor keeps 1.05 ÷ (1.05 + 0.15) = 87.5%.

pages.answer: Nothing at first, then it pulls the voltage back
pages.name: What the AVR does
options: It stops it, so the voltage holds at 100%
Nothing at first, then it pulls the voltage back
It makes it deeper, by cutting the field
pages.task: The AVR is on and watching the voltage. The motor is about to start. What does the AVR do to that first drop?
pages.why: The AVR must see the drop before it acts. Then the field takes time to grow. So a sudden step drops the voltage as far as it would with no AVR at all.[^2]

pages.name: The engine slows
pages.text: Now the engine. The start also takes 240 kW of real power, at an example power factor of 0.4. The engine cannot find that at once, so it slows. A slower rotor makes less voltage. So the dip goes deeper, to 83.8%. Then the governor adds fuel, and the speed comes back. The AVR raises the field, and the voltage climbs back to 100%. Once the motor is up to speed, its current falls away.

pages.name: A bigger motor
pages.task: The same 630 kVA set has a sub-transient reactance of 0.15 per unit. A bigger motor starts DOL and takes 900 kVA. What voltage is left at the first instant, in %, to one decimal place?

pages.alt: One 630 kVA set is on a 440 V, 60 Hz board, each with an engine and an AVR, and a second set waits off the board, drawn dashed. A motor hangs off the board behind a DOL starter, drawing 900 kVA as it starts. The motor is red: it has stalled. Two traces against time from Start to 4 s. Above, the board voltage as a % of 440 V, with a dashed line at 90%. Below, the board frequency in Hz. The voltage drops at once at Start, sags as the engine slows, then climbs as the AVR acts. The frequency dips to its lowest at 0.3 s and comes back.
pages.name: Will it get away?
pages.text: Will the motor get away? A motor's torque goes with the square of its voltage. At 90% voltage it makes 81% of its torque, enough for most loads. So the target is 90%. As the start goes on, the set's reactance grows towards its bigger synchronous reactance, here 1.5. The AVR's field has a ceiling, here an example E of 2.5. At 900 kVA, the same divider now gives 2.5 × 0.70 ÷ (0.70 + 1.5) = 79.5%. With this load, the motor stalls.

pages.name: Torque from voltage
pages.task: A start recovers the voltage to only 85%. What torque does the motor make, as a % of its full-voltage torque?
pages.why: 0.85 × 0.85 = 0.7225, about 72.3%. That is under the 81% that goes with a 90% recovery.

Above, the board voltage as a % of 440 V, with a dashed line at 90%. Below, the board frequency in Hz. The voltage drops at once at Start, sags as the engine slows, then climbs as the AVR acts. The frequency dips to its lowest at 0.3 s and comes back.
pages.name: Start softly
pages.text: The first cure is to start softly. Star-delta draws about a third of the DOL current. So 600 kVA becomes 200 kVA, and 95.5% is left at once. A soft starter's thyristors hold the current down too. In this example, it holds the start to half, 300 kVA. That leaves 93.3%. Both give the motor less torque as it starts. So they suit loads that start light, such as fans and pumps.

pages.name: Star-delta at 1,200 kVA
pages.task: The biggest motor here takes 1,200 kVA started DOL. On one set, it is started star-delta instead. What voltage is left at the first instant, in %, to one decimal place?
pages.why: The motor's impedance is 630 ÷ 400 = 1.575 per unit. 1.575 ÷ (1.575 + 0.15) = 0.913, so 91.3% is left. It recovers to 100%, and the motor gets away.

pages.alt: Two 630 kVA sets are on a 440 V, 60 Hz board, each with an engine and an AVR. A motor hangs off the board behind a DOL starter, drawing 600 kVA as it starts. Its shaft is up to speed. Two traces against time from Start to 4 s. Above, the board voltage as a % of 440 V, with a dashed line at 90%. Below, the board frequency in Hz. The voltage drops at once at Start, sags as the engine slows, then climbs as the AVR acts. The frequency dips to its lowest at 0.3 s and comes back.
pages.name: More sets on
pages.text: The second cure is more sets on the board. Two sets in parallel halve the reactance the motor sees. So the same 600 kVA start leaves 93.3%, as if each set carried 300 kVA. The drop is 6.7%, not 12.5%. They share the real power too, so the frequency dips less. A power management system can hold a big start until enough sets are on. Starting loads one at a time keeps each step small. Three motors started one after another, not together, can need 40% less starting kW.

pages.alt: Two 630 kVA sets are on a 440 V, 60 Hz board, each with an engine and an AVR. A motor hangs off the board behind a DOL starter, drawing 900 kVA as it starts. Its shaft is up to speed. pages.name: A second set at 900 kVA
pages.task: A 900 kVA DOL start stalls on one set. So you synchronise a second, identical set onto the board first. What voltage is left at the first instant now, in %, to one decimal place?
pages.why: The motor's impedance is 630 ÷ 900 = 0.70. 0.70 ÷ (0.70 + 0.075) = 0.903, so 90.3% is left. It recovers to 100%, and the motor gets away.

pages.text: Sometimes the whole board is lost. That is a blackout. The power management system works to prevent one. It sheds loads before a set is overloaded, and it holds big starts. If the board still goes dead, it recovers it. It starts the standby sets and closes them onto the dead board. Several sets can be on together, in parallel, within about 15 seconds. Then the loads come back in small steps.

pages.alt: Set A, 630 kVA, is on a live 440 V, 60 Hz board through its closed breaker. Set B, identical and up to speed, waits beside it with its breaker open, drawn dashed.
pages.answer: B must match the live board in voltage, frequency, phase sequence and angle

options: Nothing more: B can close at once, as A did

pages.task: After a blackout, set A closes onto the dead board alone and takes the first loads. Set B is now up to speed. What must happen before B's breaker closes?
pages.why: A dead board has no voltage to match, so A could close at once. Once A is on, the board is live. So B is synchronised like any set joining a live board.

pages.name: The engine's kW
pages.task: A motor's start takes 900 kVA at a power factor of 0.4. How many kW must the engine find at once?
pages.why: 900 × 0.4 = 360 kW. The governor needs a moment to add that much fuel, so the frequency dips.

pages.alt: Sets A and B, two identical 630 kVA sets, both on one 440 V, 60 Hz board, each through its own closed breaker. Each has an engine below and an AVR beside it.
pages.answer: A takes kW from B, the frequency rises, and B may be driven as a motor

pages.task: Two sets share the board in droop. Set A's governor fails and drives its fuel up. What happens?
pages.why: In parallel, more fuel on A moves kW onto A and off B. The board's frequency rises along the droop lines. If A pushes past the whole load, it drives B as a motor. B's reverse-power relay then trips it. A governor fault at one set reaches the whole board.
